concepts.title: Inflation
concepts.hook: Five ₹20 idlis fit a ₹100 note; after each idli becomes ₹25, only four fit. The note has not changed. What did?
concepts.rule: Inflation is the yearly rise in prices across a basket of everyday goods. When prices rise faster than your money, it buys less. India's central bank aims for about 4%.

claims.text: India uses a consumer price index to track change in a basket of retail prices.
A rise in broad prices cuts the buying power of cash if its amount stays fixed.
India's inflation rate compares the price of a basket this month with the same month last year. Survey staff collect the prices in markets across India.
If income rises less than prices, real income falls; people on fixed incomes lose buying power.
India's inflation target is 4%, with a low limit of 2% and a top limit of 6%, set until March 2031.

items.stem: Your college fee rises 10% a year, while your family's income rises 5% a year. What happens over a few years?

options.text: The fee takes a bigger share of income.
options.feedback: The fee grows twice as fast as income, so each year it eats a larger part of it.

options.text: Nothing changes, since both keep rising.
options.feedback: Both rise, but at different speeds. The faster one, the fee, takes a growing share.

options.text: The fee gets easier to pay.
options.feedback: Income grows slower than the fee, so paying it gets harder each year, not easier.

items.stem: Riya can keep ₹20,000 at home or in a deposit paying 7% a year. Prices rise 5%. Which keeps its buying power?

options.text: The 7% deposit.
options.feedback: It grows faster than prices, so after a year it buys a little more than today.

options.text: The cash at home.
options.feedback: Cash at home stays at ₹20,000 while prices rise 5%, so it buys less each year.

options.text: Both lose the same.
options.feedback: Only the cash falls behind. A 7% deposit outpaces 5% price rises.

items.stem: A toy cost ₹385 last May and ₹410 this May. What is its inflation rate?

options.text: About 6.5%.
options.feedback: The rise is ₹25. Divide 25 by last May's ₹385 and multiply by 100 to get about 6.5%.

options.text: About 25%.
options.feedback: ₹25 is the rise in rupees, not the percent. Divide it by ₹385 to get about 6.5%.

options.text: About 0.65%.
options.feedback: The decimal point slipped. 25 divided by 385 is about 0.065, which is 6.5%.

items.stem: How does India find out what prices are doing each month?

options.text: Survey staff note prices in towns and villages.
options.feedback: Yes. Every month, survey staff record retail prices in markets across India, in towns and in villages.

options.text: Shops send one price list a year.
options.feedback: Prices are recorded every month, not once a year, and survey staff collect them in person.

options.text: It guesses from a few big cities.
options.feedback: No guessing is involved. Survey staff record prices every month in markets across India, in villages as well as cities.

items.stem: Why do people living on a fixed pension feel rising prices the most?

options.text: Their income stays put while prices climb.
options.feedback: A pension that never grows meets higher prices each year, so it buys less and less.

options.text: Pensions rise faster than prices.
options.feedback: A fixed pension does not rise at all, so it falls behind when prices go up.

options.text: Older people buy different goods.
options.feedback: Their shopping may differ, but the main problem is income that stays fixed while prices rise.

items.stem: Pay counted in rupees is nominal pay. Pay counted by what it can buy is ___.

options.text: Real pay.
options.feedback: Pay measured by what it buys is called real pay. It shows how far the money really goes.

options.text: Rupee pay.
options.feedback: That is the nominal figure again, the rupee amount, not what the money can buy.

options.text: Old pay.
options.feedback: Last year's pay is still counted in rupees. Adjusting pay for prices gives real pay.

items.stem: A friend says any inflation at all means the economy is in trouble. What is wrong with that?

options.text: India even aims for about 4%.
options.feedback: The RBI's target is 4% inflation, with a band of 2% to 6%, so mild inflation is planned.

options.text: The RBI wants zero inflation.
options.feedback: The target is not zero. It is 4%, with a lower limit of 2%.

options.text: Prices should stay fixed forever.
options.feedback: No target asks for fixed prices. India aims for steady rises of about 4% a year.

items.stem: Put these in order to work out an inflation rate.

options.text: Find this May's price and last May's price.
options.feedback: You need the same item's price in the same month, one year apart, before any sum.

options.text: Subtract to get the rise in rupees.
options.feedback: The gap between the two prices shows how many rupees more it costs now.

options.text: Divide the rise by last May's price, then multiply by 100.
options.feedback: Dividing by the older price turns the rupee rise into a percent, the inflation rate.

misconceptions.name: One price is the index
misconceptions.correction: One snack can rise while the broad basket moves in a different way.

misconceptions.name: Same cash, same goods
misconceptions.correction: When broad prices rise, the same cash can buy fewer goods.

misconceptions.name: Any raise makes you better off
misconceptions.correction: A raise smaller than the rise in prices still buys less than before.

misconceptions.name: The goal is zero inflation
misconceptions.correction: India's target is about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

steps.title: Inflation is prices rising across a basket

hook.stem: The news says retail inflation was 3% in May. What does that mean?

options.text: Everyday prices are about 3% above last May.
options.feedback: Right. It compares a big basket of everyday prices with the same month a year before.

options.text: Every single price rose by exactly 3%.
options.feedback: Some prices jump and some barely move. The 3% is the overall change across the basket.

options.text: Prices rose 3% since April.
options.feedback: The figure compares this May with last May, a full year apart, not with the month before.

steps.teach: Inflation is how much prices rose in a year. India checks a basket of everyday goods each month and compares it with the same month last year.

parts: Rice, milk and bus fares in the big list
cost 3% more than they did last May,
example.spot: cost 3% more than they did last May,
example.feedback: Inflation compares the same basket with the same month a year earlier.

guided.stem: Onions double in price, but most other prices barely move. What happens to inflation?
guided.hint: Onions are one item in a very big basket.

options.text: It goes up a little.
options.feedback: Yes. One item doubling moves the whole basket only a little when the rest stays flat.

options.text: It doubles too.
options.feedback: Onions are a small part of the basket, so the overall rise is far smaller than double.

options.text: It falls.
options.feedback: A price went up and the others held still, so the basket costs a bit more, not less.

guided.stem: This June's inflation figure is out. Which prices does it compare?
guided.hint: Look for a gap of one full year.

options.text: This June against last June.
options.feedback: Right. Matching the same month a year apart is how the rate is worked out.

options.text: This June against this May.
options.feedback: A one-month gap is not used here. The rate compares the same month a year earlier.

options.text: This June against ten years ago.
options.feedback: Ten years is far too long a gap. The yearly rate compares with the same month last year.

steps.takeaway: Inflation is the yearly rise across a whole basket of prices.

steps.title: When prices outrun your money, it buys less

hook.stem: Your pocket money stays at ₹2,000 while prices rise 10%. What happens?

options.text: It buys about a tenth less.
options.feedback: Right. The note is the same, but each thing costs more, so the same money covers less.

options.text: It buys the same, since it is still ₹2,000.
options.feedback: The number on the money stays put, but prices moved up, so it now covers less shopping.

options.text: It buys 10% more.
options.feedback: Higher prices work the other way. The same ₹2,000 now covers less, not more.

steps.teach: When prices rise, the same money buys less. If your income grows slower than prices, you can buy less than last year, even with a raise.

parts: Kavya got a 5% raise this year,
but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
so her pay now buys less than before.
example.spot: but her rent and groceries cost 7% more,
example.feedback: Her costs grew faster than her pay, so the raise did not keep up.

guided.stem: A ₹100 basket of shopping now costs ₹125. How much of it does ₹100 buy?

options.text: Four fifths of it.
options.feedback: Yes. 100 divided by 125 is 0.8, so the same cash covers 80% of the basket.

options.text: All of it.
options.feedback: The basket now costs ₹125, more than you hold, so ₹100 cannot cover all of it.

options.text: One and a quarter baskets.
options.feedback: That flips the sum. ₹125 is the new price, so ₹100 buys less than one basket.

guided.stem: Prices rise 5% this year. Whose pay keeps up?
guided.hint: Pay has to grow at least as fast as prices.

options.text: Arjun's, up 6%.
options.feedback: Right. His pay grew faster than prices, so it buys a little more than last year.

options.text: Meena's, up 3%.
options.feedback: Her pay rose, but slower than prices, so it buys less than it did last year.

options.text: Ravi's, unchanged.
options.feedback: With no rise at all, his same pay meets higher prices and buys less.

steps.takeaway: If prices grow faster than your money, you fall behind.

steps.title: Idle cash shrinks, and the RBI aims for about 4%

hook.stem: What inflation rate do you think India's central bank aims for?

options.text: About 4%.
options.feedback: Right. The RBI's target is 4%, with a band from 2% to 6% around it.

options.text: Zero.
options.feedback: The target is not zero. India aims for about 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

options.text: 10% or more.
options.feedback: That would be far above the band. The upper limit is 6%, and the target is 4%.

steps.teach: Money that earns nothing loses buying power each year. India's central bank aims to keep inflation near 4%, inside a band of 2% to 6%.

example.ask: Tap what happens to the cash.
parts: Dadaji keeps ₹50,000 under his mattress for years,
and each year it buys a little less,
because prices keep rising around it.
example.spot: and each year it buys a little less,
example.feedback: The cash never changes, but rising prices make it worth a little less each year.

guided.stem: ₹10,000 sits in a cupboard for a year while prices rise 5%. What does it buy next year?
guided.hint: The cash stays still while prices move up.

options.text: About what ₹9,500 buys today.
options.feedback: Yes. 10,000 divided by 1.05 is about 9,520, so it buys a bit less than now.

options.text: Exactly what ₹10,000 buys today.
options.feedback: Prices rose 5% while the cash stayed the same, so it buys less than it does today.

options.text: About what ₹10,500 buys today.
options.feedback: Cash in a cupboard earns nothing. Rising prices make it buy less, not more.

guided.stem: Inflation comes in at 7% this year. Where is that against the RBI's band?

options.text: Above the 6% upper limit.
options.feedback: Right. 7% is higher than the 6% upper limit of the band.

options.text: Right on target.
options.feedback: The target is 4%. At 7%, inflation is above even the 6% upper limit.

options.text: Below the lower limit.
options.feedback: The lower limit is 2%. A rate of 7% is well above the whole band.

steps.takeaway: Idle cash shrinks; India aims for about 4% inflation.

concepts.title: Compounding
concepts.hook: ₹1 lakh growing at a made-up 7% for 30 years becomes about ₹7.6 lakh. The last ten years add more than the first twenty.
concepts.rule: Compounding means a gain can earn a later gain when it stays in the pot. A SIP adds money at set times, but that does not promise a set return.

claims.text: Compound growth includes growth on past gains as well as the starting amount.
A SIP is a way to add money at set times; market returns are not fixed.

items.stem: Riya's family shop earns ₹100 interest on ₹1,000 and leaves it in. What earns interest next time?

options.text: Both the ₹1,000 and the ₹100.
options.feedback: Once a gain stays in the account, later growth can apply to that larger total.

options.text: Only the ₹1,000; the ₹100 never counts.
options.feedback: The first ₹1,000 is easy to track. The saved ₹100 is now in the base too.

options.text: Nothing; interest is paid just once.
options.feedback: Interest keeps arriving at the same rate. Each time, it builds on the larger total left in the account.

items.stem: Two hostel clubs earn the same rate. Club A takes gains out; Club B leaves them in. Which earns on past gains?

options.text: Club B, which leaves gains in.
options.feedback: Retained gains join the amount on which the next rate is applied.

options.text: Club A, which takes gains out.
options.feedback: Withdrawing gains keeps them out of the next rate base, even though both clubs use the same rate.

options.text: Both earn the same on past gains.
options.feedback: Only kept gains join the base. The club that withdraws its gains earns nothing on them next year.

items.stem: ₹100 earns 10% in year one and the ₹10 gain stays in. About how much gain comes in year two?

options.feedback: The second gain applies to ₹110 because the first gain stayed in the account.
The first gain was ₹10, so it is easy to reuse. The saved ₹10 earns more too.
That doubles the first gain. Ten percent of ₹110 is ₹11, so the second year adds ₹11.

items.stem: An exam club adds ₹100 to a fund each month. Which part is a payment plan, not a promised return?

options.text: Adding ₹100 every month.
options.feedback: The schedule says when money enters; it cannot set what markets later pay.

options.text: A monthly payment makes the fund rise monthly.
options.feedback: A steady pay date can feel like steady growth. The fund price can still fall.

options.text: A fixed return from each payment.
options.feedback: A set pay date can feel like a set gain. Yet the fund may rise or fall.

items.stem: Two equal accounts earn the same steady rate. One keeps its gains; one takes them out. Why does the first grow more?

options.text: Kept gains also earn interest.
options.feedback: The same percentage applies to a larger balance when earlier gains remain in the account.

options.text: Both grow by the same rupees each year.
options.feedback: The common rate makes this sound fair. Saved gains grow the base in only one account.

options.text: Its rate rises each year.
options.feedback: Larger gains can look like a higher rate. A steady rate also makes more on a larger base.

items.stem: ₹200 grows to ₹220, and the ₹20 stays in. Next year's 10% is worked out on ___.

options.feedback: The saved gain has joined the base, which is the key step in compounding.
The starting sum sticks in mind. The saved ₹20 also joins the new base.
The gain alone is too small a base. The next 10% is worked out on the full ₹220.

items.stem: A chart shows money growing 10% every year. Neha expects a real share to do the same. What is wrong?

options.text: A real share's return can change each year.
options.feedback: The chart assumes the same gain every year. A real share's value can go up or down from year to year.

options.text: Nothing: past gains make the next gain certain.
options.feedback: A rising line can invite that guess. A real share can lose value next year.

options.text: Nothing: the chart's steady rate will carry on.
options.feedback: The smooth chart makes the rate look dependable, but a real share's return can change; compounding alone promises no path.

items.stem: Match each amount to its job in a savings account.

options.text: Starting ₹100
options.feedback: This sum came first. It is the base on which the first gain is worked out.

options.text: Base for the first gain
options.feedback: The first base is present before any gain has been added to the account.

options.text: Saved ₹10 gain
options.feedback: This gain stays in the account, so it can join the amount used for the next gain.

options.text: Part of the next base
options.feedback: The later rate can act on this saved gain as well as the first sum.

misconceptions.name: Gain only on start
misconceptions.correction: When gains stay in the pot, later gains can build on them too.

misconceptions.name: SIP means sure gain
misconceptions.correction: A SIP sets a payment pattern; it does not set market returns.

concepts.title: The rule of 72
concepts.hook: At a made-up 9% rate, 72 ÷ 9 says eight years to double. Working it out exactly gives close to eight, but not exactly eight.
concepts.rule: For a steady percent gain, divide 72 by the rate to guess the years to double. It is a rough math shortcut, not a promise of market growth.

claims.text: The rule of 72 is a rough way to guess when a sum may double. Divide 72 by a set rate.
Market returns do not have a fixed rate, so the shortcut is only a what-if tool there.

items.stem: A hostel quiz uses a steady 8% growth rate. By the rule of 72, about when does money double?

options.text: About nine years.
options.feedback: The shortcut divides 72 by eight, then treats the answer as a rough time.

options.text: Eight years.
options.feedback: Eight is the rate, so it is tempting to call it years. Divide 72 by 8 instead.

options.text: About 72 years.
options.feedback: Seventy-two is the number you divide, not the answer. Divided by 8, it gives about nine years.

items.stem: On a train, Arjun compares two steady rates: 6% and 9%. Which one doubles money sooner?

options.text: The 9% case.
options.feedback: A larger assumed rate makes 72 divided by that rate smaller.

options.text: The 6% case.
options.feedback: Six can look like the shorter wait. As a rate, it grows money more slowly than nine.

options.text: Both take the same time.
options.feedback: Different rates give different waits. 72 ÷ 9 is 8 years, while 72 ÷ 6 is 12 years.

items.stem: A steady rate drops from 6% to 3%. By the rule of 72, about how many years to double now?

options.text: 24 years.
options.feedback: The lower steady rate gives a longer rough doubling time; the shortcut uses the new rate.

options.text: 12 years.
options.feedback: Twelve years fit the old 6% rate. At 3%, the rough wait is twice as long.

options.text: 6 years.
options.feedback: A lower rate makes doubling slower, not faster. 72 ÷ 3 gives about 24 years.

items.stem: A class chart shows a rate that changes every year. How should you read its rule-of-72 answer?

options.text: As a rough guess if the rate held steady.
options.feedback: The shortcut assumes one rate, so a changing path may reach double at another time.

options.text: As the true answer, using this year's rate.
options.feedback: A current rate is easy to plug in. The shortcut needs it to stay steady for the guess.

options.text: As a sure date for doubling.
options.feedback: A neat number can feel like a date. If rates move, the true wait can change too.

items.stem: One balance grows at a steady 12%, another at 4%. Why does the rule of 72 give different times?

options.text: A higher rate needs fewer years.
options.feedback: Dividing 72 by a larger rate gives a shorter rough time, assuming each rate stays steady.

options.text: The 12% one takes longer, since it earns more.
options.feedback: More gain can sound like more time. At a steady rate, more gain means a shorter wait.

options.text: A bigger starting balance doubles faster.
options.feedback: More starting cash means more rupees gained, but the rule works out doubling time from the percent rate alone.

items.stem: At a steady 3% rate, the rule gives 72 ÷ 3 = ___.

options.text: About 24 years.
options.feedback: A low rate makes the time to double long. The rule still gives only a rough answer.

options.text: About 3 years.
options.feedback: Three is the rate, so it is easy to reuse. The rule asks for 72 divided by 3.

options.text: About 216 years.
options.feedback: That multiplies instead of dividing. The rule asks for 72 ÷ 3, which is about 24 years.

items.stem: A rate is 8% this year and 4% next year. Sam says 72 ÷ 8 proves nine years to double. What is wrong?

options.text: The rule needs a rate that stays steady.
options.feedback: A rate that keeps changing breaks the shortcut, and even a steady rate gives only a rough answer.

options.text: The rule averages the two rates itself.
options.feedback: A quick rule may seem to handle changes. Here it uses one assumed steady rate.

options.text: This year's 8% can stand for every year.
options.feedback: Using this year's rate gives a quick guess, but the shortcut needs the rate to stay steady. Next year's 4% breaks that.

items.stem: Why is this shortcut useful in class?

options.text: It turns a rate into a quick doubling guess.
options.feedback: You can do this sum in your head. A full growth sum may give a different time.

options.text: It proves a return will stay fixed.
options.feedback: The rule gives one clean number. Real rates can change, so the guess is not a promise.

options.text: It tells the day money doubles.
options.feedback: The shortcut gives a rough guess, not a date. Real growth sums and changing rates can differ.

misconceptions.name: Exact clock
misconceptions.correction: The rule gives a rough guess, not an exact date.

misconceptions.name: Any market rate is fixed
misconceptions.correction: Market gains can vary; the shortcut needs a steady assumed rate.

concepts.title: Risk and return
concepts.hook: A fair coin pays ₹30 on heads and nothing on tails; a sure ₹12 ticket pays less at best but never zero. The range matters.
concepts.rule: A bigger possible gain often comes with more chance of loss or a wider range of results. A high possible return is not a sure return.

claims.text: Investment risk includes the chance of loss and uncertain results.
A high possible gain may mean more risk. The gain is not sure.

items.stem: At a school fair, Game A pays ₹30 or ₹0. Game B always pays ₹12. Which has the wider spread?

options.text: Game A.
options.feedback: Its two possible payouts are far apart, so you are less sure what you will get.

options.text: Game B, the sure one.
options.feedback: The sure prize may look safer and larger than zero. Its best and worst result are still the same.

options.text: Both are the same.
options.feedback: One game always pays ₹12. The other swings from ₹0 to ₹30, so its range is much wider.

items.stem: In exam week, a family shop spends money making a new snack. Which result is possible?

options.text: A loss or a gain.
options.feedback: Some snacks may not sell. A big best case does not tell us how many buyers will come.

options.text: Its costs come back even if sales are slow.
options.feedback: A busy shop can make some sales seem likely, but unsold stock can leave the owner with a loss.

options.text: Only a gain, since exam week brings buyers.
options.feedback: Exam weeks can bring buyers, but nothing makes sales sure. Unsold stock can turn the plan into a loss.

items.stem: A ₹30 raffle ticket has a 1-in-4 chance to win ₹100. After its cost, what is the average return?

options.text: A loss of ₹5.
options.feedback: The average payout is ₹25, below the ₹30 cost, even though one outcome pays ₹100.

options.text: A gain of ₹70.
options.feedback: The ₹100 prize stands out. The three losing tickets also count in the average.

options.text: No gain or loss: ₹0.
options.feedback: The average payout is ₹25, below the ₹30 ticket. On average, each ticket ends ₹5 down.

items.stem: A poster shows only the best possible prize. What does it leave out about risk?

options.text: How often bad results happen, and how bad.
options.feedback: A maximum alone leaves out how often that amount occurs and what losses remain possible.

options.text: How big the best prize is next to the cost.
options.feedback: A large best-case payout catches attention, but risk also depends on the other outcomes and their chances.

options.text: The name of the prize sponsor.
options.feedback: Who pays the prize says little about risk. What matters is how often poor results happen and how bad they are.

items.stem: A poster says a share could gain 30%, and shows nothing else. Why can't you know its average return?

options.text: One possible gain is not all the outcomes.
options.feedback: To find an average, we need the other possible gains and losses, plus their chances.

options.text: A possible 30% gain is the average.
options.feedback: The headline gain stands out. An average also needs the other results and their chances.

options.text: Holding longer makes 30% the average.
options.feedback: A long hold can seem to smooth risk. It still does not tell us the other outcomes.

items.stem: ₹10 for sure has a narrow range. ₹0 or ₹30 has a ___.

options.text: Wider range of results.
options.feedback: The second payoff can land at either extreme, making its result less predictable.

options.text: Higher average payoff.
options.feedback: The possible ₹30 prize looks larger than ₹10, but one branch pays nothing; the range alone cannot establish the average.

options.text: Lower chance of zero.
options.feedback: The ₹0 branch makes a zero more likely, not less. What the second option clearly has is a wider spread.

items.stem: Two games have the same average payout, but one has wider results. Ravi says it must pay more. What is wrong?

options.text: Wider results can include lower ones.
options.feedback: More variation changes the risk of each result; it does not raise the stated average by itself.

options.text: Same average means the same lowest payout.
options.feedback: A shared average can hide the spread. One game can still have a much worse low result.

options.text: A higher top prize forces the average up.
options.feedback: The high prize draws the eye. Lower results can offset it, leaving the same average.

items.stem: What trade does the fair-game example show?

options.text: A bigger possible prize comes with more spread.
options.feedback: Comparing both good and bad outcomes shows what the attractive headline hides.

options.text: Only the biggest prize counts.
options.feedback: The top prize is easy to picture. A zero result is also possible and widens the spread.

options.text: A sure prize is the better choice.
options.feedback: The example compares spread, not which is better. A sure prize narrows the range but caps the gain.

misconceptions.name: High means sure
misconceptions.correction: A high possible return can come with a loss too.

misconceptions.name: No loss is possible
misconceptions.correction: An uncertain asset can lose value as well as gain it.

concepts.title: Diversification
concepts.hook: A monsoon cancels cricket practice and hurts both a bat seller and a ball seller. Two products can still share one shock.
concepts.rule: Spreading money across different holdings can cut the harm from one weak part. It cannot make all loss go away, since many parts can fall together.

claims.text: A mix of holdings can spread the risk from one firm.
A broad mix can cut some risk from one firm. It cannot wipe out all risk.

items.stem: A family shop sells only mango juice. Monsoon rain keeps buyers away. What happens to its sales?

options.text: All its sales take the hit.
options.feedback: With one product, there is no other product line to offset that missing demand.

options.text: Regular buyers keep sales steady.
options.feedback: Loyal buyers can soften a bad day, but a shop with only one line has no other product to offset a juice slump.

options.text: Sales shift to its other products.
options.feedback: There are no other products to shift to. With one line, the rain hits all of the shop's sales.

items.stem: At a college fest, Stall A sells juice and snacks; Stall B sells only juice. Fruit prices jump. Which stall has a backup?

options.text: Stall A, with juice and snacks.
options.feedback: A separate product gives it one source of sales that does not use the costly fruit.

options.text: Stall B, with only juice.
options.feedback: A juice stall can seem focused and strong. It has no fruit-free line to lean on.

options.text: Both are hit equally.
options.feedback: Only the juice-only stall depends fully on fruit. The other has snacks that do not use fruit.

items.stem: Four holdings are different businesses in one flood zone. A flood hits. How many does business type protect?

options.text: 0 holdings.
options.feedback: Different lines of business do not remove a location risk shared by all four.

options.text: 3 holdings.
options.feedback: Different businesses may face different sales risks, but one flood can reach all four shops.

options.text: 4 holdings.
options.feedback: Business type does not stop a flood. All four shops sit in the same zone, so none is shielded.

items.stem: Sana owns four firms in different businesses, but all need the same crop. What risk is still there?

options.text: A bad harvest hurting all four.
options.feedback: All four firms need the crop, so a poor harvest can hurt the whole mix.

options.text: One firm's own bad decision.
options.feedback: Owning several firms cuts the harm from one firm's mistake. Here the shared crop is a risk to the whole mix.

options.text: None, since there are four firms.
options.feedback: Four firms can still share one weak spot. Here a bad harvest can hit every firm at once.

items.stem: One holding crashes while the others hold steady. Why does spreading money help here, but not with every shock?

options.text: Only part of the mix is hit.
options.feedback: Other holdings can cushion one firm’s loss, while a shared shock may still reach several.

options.text: A mix protects against shocks hitting all firms.
options.feedback: Spread can help with one firm's loss. A shared shock can still pull all holdings down.

options.text: Each holding cancels the others' losses.
options.feedback: More names can feel like a hedge. A shared shock may pull them down together.

items.stem: Spreading money limits the harm from one firm. What loss can still hit the whole mix?

options.text: A loss that hits many holdings at once.
options.feedback: A big shock can pull many holdings down together, even when no single firm is a large part of the mix.

options.text: Only a loss at one company.
options.feedback: Spreading holdings can limit one firm's damage, but a shared market shock can still reach the whole mix.

options.text: None, once you hold ten.
options.feedback: More holdings can cut single-firm harm, but not shared shocks. A broad market fall can still reach the mix.

items.stem: Amit owns ten firms that all need one crop. He says the different names keep him fully safe. What risk remains?

options.text: A bad crop can hurt all ten.
options.feedback: Many firms can share one driver, so their losses can arrive together.

options.text: Ten names make sure one escapes.
options.feedback: Many names look spread out. Here each business still needs the same crop.

options.text: Equal amounts in each remove the crop risk.
options.feedback: Equal weights look well spread. They still leave each firm tied to the crop.

items.stem: Which line explains why a mix of holdings can still fall?

options.text: It cuts one-firm risk, not every loss.
options.feedback: The mix matters because weak parts may differ, while a common shock can still hurt all.

options.text: It can't; a mix removes all risk of a fall.
options.feedback: Many holdings can feel safe. A broad market fall can reach much of the mix.

options.text: Only when one holding drops to zero.
options.feedback: Losses can come without any holding hitting zero. A common shock can push many parts down a little at once.

misconceptions.name: One basket is enough
misconceptions.correction: One firm or sector leaves a lot tied to one outcome.

misconceptions.name: Many means no loss
misconceptions.correction: Many holdings can still fall at the same time.

sources.title: Beginners Guide to Asset Allocation, Diversification, and Rebalancing
sources.publisher: Investor.gov, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission

concepts.title: What a stock is
concepts.hook: One share makes a student a tiny owner of a company. It does not promise a fixed payment or any dividend.
concepts.rule: A share is a small ownership claim in a company. Its price can change; a dividend may be paid, but neither a gain nor a dividend is assured.

claims.text: A share gives part ownership of a company.
A firm may pay a share of its gains. The payout is not sure.

items.stem: In a family shop lesson, Asha gets one share in a firm. What does it give her?

options.text: A small part of owning the firm.
options.feedback: Ownership can link its value to the firm, while future price and payouts remain uncertain.

options.text: A fixed payout every year.
options.feedback: Owners may get a payout, so it can sound owed. A firm may pay none.

options.text: A loan she made to the firm.
options.feedback: Both can fund a firm, so they are easy to mix up. A share gives ownership, not a loan claim.

items.stem: At the hostel, Kiran owns shares in a firm. It pays no dividend (profit payout) this year. Is he still an owner?

options.text: Yes, he still owns part of it.
options.feedback: A dividend is a possible payout, not the test for whether a share represents ownership.

options.text: No, no payout cancels the share.
options.feedback: A dividend can feel like proof of ownership. The share still exists when none is paid.

options.text: Only until the price falls.
options.feedback: A falling price changes what the share is worth, not who owns it. The holder remains an owner.

items.stem: Nisha owns 5 of a company's 100 shares. The share price halves; no new shares are made. What percent does she own?

options.feedback: A price fall changes the holding’s market value, not the fraction of unchanged shares she owns.
The price fell by half, so 2.5% looks natural. Her share count stayed five out of 100.
Her share count did not change, so her fraction did not double. She still owns 5 of the 100 shares.

items.stem: A cricket club sells match tickets and ownership shares. Which one gives a claim on the club itself?

options.text: The ownership share.
options.feedback: The share links the holder to the enterprise; a ticket grants a service instead.

options.text: The ticket, since it funds the club.
options.feedback: A ticket helps club revenue, but it buys entry to an event rather than an ownership claim.

options.text: Both, equally.
options.feedback: A ticket buys entry to an event. Only the share gives a claim of ownership in the club.

items.stem: A company pays a dividend, but its share price still falls. How can both happen?

options.text: Price and dividend are separate things.
options.feedback: Ownership can bring a dividend without guaranteeing what later buyers will pay for the share.

options.text: The dividend always makes up for the drop.
options.feedback: Cash paid out can feel like a safety net. Its size need not match a market fall.

options.text: Any dividend keeps the price above the old one.
options.feedback: The cash payout feels like a gain. Buyers can still set a lower share price.

items.stem: Some companies pay owners part of their profit. That payment is called a ___.

options.text: Dividend.
options.feedback: It can transfer part of profit to owners, but a firm need not declare one.

options.text: Fixed interest payment.
options.feedback: Both can pay cash, so the names are easy to mix up. A share may pay a dividend.

options.text: Loan.
options.feedback: Money lent is paid back with interest. Profit paid out to owners is called a dividend.

items.stem: A company paid a dividend last year. Dev plans on the same monthly payout this year. What is wrong?

options.text: Past payouts do not promise new ones.
options.feedback: The firm may pay less, or nothing. Owning shares does not promise cash each month.

options.text: Last year's payout sets a minimum for this year.
options.feedback: Past cash can feel like a pattern. The firm can pay less or none this year.

options.text: Last year's payout is now a fixed monthly debt.
options.feedback: Last year's payout can look like a schedule. Ownership does not make it a fixed monthly debt.

items.stem: Which line explains what a share is?

options.text: Part ownership, with a changing price and possible payouts.
options.feedback: The two ways to get a return can vary, and neither is built in as a guarantee.

options.text: A loan with a fixed due date and yearly payout.
options.feedback: Both raise money for a firm. A share is ownership and has no fixed loan due date.

options.text: A coupon for discounts at the firm.
options.feedback: Some firms offer perks, but that is not what a share is. A share is part ownership with an uncertain price.

misconceptions.name: Share is a loan
misconceptions.correction: A share is ownership, not a fixed loan payment.

misconceptions.name: Dividend is owed
misconceptions.correction: A firm may pay a dividend; it is not automatic.

concepts.title: Emergency fund
concepts.hook: A sudden repair bill is easier to meet when money is already set aside and easy to reach.
concepts.rule: An emergency fund is money kept for an unexpected need. Its useful feature is ready access when the need arrives.

claims.text: An emergency fund is cash kept for a sudden need.
The reserve is useful when it can be reached without waiting for a sale.

items.stem: A hostel student gets a sudden phone repair bill. Which money can pay it right away?

options.text: Cash kept aside for surprises.
options.feedback: A ready reserve can cover an unplanned bill while other plans stay separate.

options.text: An item she plans to sell next week.
options.feedback: Resale value can look like savings, but a bill due today needs money the student can reach now.

options.text: A fixed deposit that ends next year.
options.feedback: Locked money may not be ready today. A cash reserve kept aside can pay the bill at once.

items.stem: In exam week, the family shop's fridge breaks. Which savings count as an emergency fund?

options.text: Money kept for a surprise repair.
options.feedback: The repair was not on the normal bill list, so a ready reserve fits.

options.text: Money saved for next month's rent.
options.feedback: Rent money is saved, so it may look like a reserve. The bill is known in advance.

options.text: Money saved for a planned holiday.
options.feedback: A holiday is a plan, not a surprise. An emergency fund is for costs like a sudden fridge repair.

items.stem: An emergency fund holds one month's cash and a cricket card worth one month. How many months can pay today?

options.text: One month.
options.feedback: The cash can pay today. The card would need a buyer first.

options.text: Two months.
options.feedback: The card has a price, so two months looks fair. It needs a buyer before the bill is due.

options.text: Zero months.
options.feedback: The cash is ready and can pay today. Only the card needs a buyer first, so one month is ready.

items.stem: What matters most about money kept for a sudden bill?

options.text: Easy to reach.
options.feedback: A surprise bill needs money that can be reached when the bill arrives.

options.text: Invested for the highest return.
options.feedback: Growth sounds useful for savings, but a sudden expense calls for money that can be accessed promptly.

options.text: Hidden away.
options.feedback: Out of sight can help, but the key feature is being reachable. A sudden bill needs money that is easy to get.

items.stem: Kabir has valuable cricket cards but no cash. Why is a sudden bill still hard to pay?

options.text: The cards first need a buyer.
options.feedback: Value on paper does not put money in hand on the bill date.

options.text: A card's listed price is cash today.
options.feedback: A price tag makes value look real. The card still needs a buyer before it pays a bill.

options.text: Any valuable thing works like cash.
options.feedback: The card may be worth a lot. A buyer still has to turn that value into cash.

items.stem: A monthly bus pass is a planned cost. A sudden repair is ___.

options.text: An unexpected cost.
options.feedback: The repair arrives without a set date, which is the kind of need the reserve covers.

options.text: A normal monthly bill.
options.feedback: Both cost money, so they can seem alike. The repair was not planned each month.

options.text: A savings goal.
options.feedback: Goals are planned on purpose. A sudden repair comes without warning, so it is an unexpected cost.

items.stem: Neha says emergency savings only matter if they earn the most. What is she missing?

options.text: Being able to reach it in a surprise.
options.feedback: A high return says little about whether the money can pay an urgent bill.

options.text: Selling later is fine for a bill due now.
options.feedback: A sale may bring cash later. A sudden bill needs funds that can be reached today.

options.text: A high return gives instant cash.
options.feedback: A high gain feels useful. It may come in an asset that cannot pay a bill today.

items.stem: How would you explain an emergency fund to a friend?

options.text: Ready money for costs that come without warning.
options.feedback: The key is a separate reserve that can meet an unplanned need.

options.text: Money set aside for a known monthly bill.
options.feedback: Both pools are set aside. A known bill belongs in the plan, while a surprise does not.

options.text: Money for sales and deals.
options.feedback: Sale spending is a choice, not a surprise need. The fund is ready money for costs that come without warning.

misconceptions.name: Any savings will do
misconceptions.correction: Money tied up in a hard-to-sell asset may not be ready when an urgent bill arrives.

misconceptions.name: Every planned bill is an emergency
misconceptions.correction: A known monthly bill is planned spending, while an emergency is unexpected.

quest.title: Sort a bill
quest.detail: Name a planned bill and a surprise bill in a made-up hostel budget.

concepts.title: EMI and loan cost
concepts.hook: A smaller monthly EMI can still lead to more total interest when a loan runs longer.
concepts.rule: An EMI pays interest and some principal. On a reducing balance, interest is based on what is still owed.

claims.text: An EMI can pay loan interest and part of the loan sum.
As a loan shrinks, later interest uses the sum still due.

items.stem: A family shop pays a loan EMI (fixed monthly payment). Part of it cuts the debt. What happens next month?

options.text: Interest is charged on a smaller debt.
options.feedback: The lender works out later interest from what is still owed, not the old balance.

options.text: Interest is still charged on the first amount.
options.feedback: The first loan sum is easy to recall. Paid principal is no longer part of the balance.

options.text: The EMI doubles.
options.feedback: A fixed EMI usually stays the same. What changes is the split: less goes to interest as the balance falls.

items.stem: A college student compares two loans at the same rate. One spreads payments over more months. What happens?

options.text: Each EMI is smaller, but total interest is higher.
options.feedback: More payment months can make each bill smaller while interest runs for longer.

options.text: Both the EMI and total interest fall.
options.feedback: A lower EMI feels cheaper today. More months can still add to the total interest.

options.text: Total interest falls, since each EMI is smaller.
options.feedback: Smaller payments over more months keep interest running longer. Total interest tends to rise, not fall.

items.stem: You borrow ₹10,000 and repay 12 EMIs of ₹900. About how much of that is interest?

options.text: About ₹800.
options.feedback: Twelve payments of ₹900 total ₹10,800. Subtract the ₹10,000 borrowed to get ₹800 interest.

options.text: About ₹900.
options.feedback: One EMI is ₹900, but interest is part of all 12 payments. Total paid minus principal is ₹800.
₹10,800 is all you pay. Take away the ₹10,000 loan to get ₹800 in interest.

items.stem: In a loan, what is the principal?

options.text: The loan money still owed.
options.feedback: Paying down principal reduces the amount on which later interest can be worked out.

options.text: The full EMI paid each month.
options.feedback: The EMI is what you pay each month. The principal is the debt left to repay.

options.text: The interest rate on the loan.
options.feedback: The rate is a percentage charged on the debt. Principal is the loan money still owed.

items.stem: Two loans have the same EMI, but one runs for more months. Why can their total costs differ?

options.text: The number of payments matters too.
options.feedback: One monthly figure hides how many times it is paid and how long interest runs.

options.text: The longer loan costs less, since EMIs match.
options.feedback: The matching bill looks fair. More months can still add up to a larger total.

options.text: Same EMI means the same total cost.
options.feedback: A matching EMI feels like a matching deal. Extra months can raise the total paid.

items.stem: Each EMI pays off some of the loan. That leaves a smaller ___ to charge interest on.

options.text: Amount still owed.
options.feedback: The remaining debt, rather than the first borrowed amount, becomes the next base.

options.text: First amount borrowed.
options.feedback: The first loan sum sticks in mind. Yet each payment cuts the debt used for new interest.

options.text: Interest rate.
options.feedback: Paying principal does not change the rate. It lowers the balance that the next interest charge is based on.

items.stem: Ravi says every rupee of his EMI pays off the loan amount. What is wrong?

options.text: Part of each EMI pays interest.
options.feedback: A loan table shows what pays debt and what pays interest each month.

options.text: Every EMI cuts the debt by its full amount.
options.feedback: The debt does fall, so this sounds right. Part of a payment can cover interest.

options.text: All of it pays debt; interest comes at the end.
options.feedback: The debt is paid in parts, so interest may seem like a final fee. It can sit in each EMI.

items.stem: Which line best sums up how EMI interest works?

options.text: Interest follows the debt still unpaid.
options.feedback: As debt goes down, the next interest charge starts from less.

options.text: Interest uses the first amount borrowed.
options.feedback: The first loan sum is easy to use. In this method, later interest uses the debt still owed.

options.text: Interest is paid only at the end.
options.feedback: Each EMI pays some interest as it goes. When the debt shrinks, the next interest charge shrinks too.

misconceptions.name: EMI is all principal
misconceptions.correction: Part of a typical EMI pays interest, while the rest lowers the debt.

misconceptions.name: Small EMI means cheap loan
misconceptions.correction: A longer term can lower each payment but raise total interest.

sources.title: RBI housing loan FAQs: reducing balance and amortization

quest.title: Read a schedule
quest.detail: In a sample EMI table, point to the principal, interest and balance columns.

concepts.title: Index funds and stock picking
concepts.hook: An index fund holds a whole basket of companies. One chosen stock rides on a single company.
concepts.rule: An index fund aims to track an index after costs. Picking one stock is a different bet on one firm.

claims.text: An index fund holds securities to follow a named index and charges an expense ratio.
Past India fund data show many active funds below their index. The share varies by year and fund group.

items.stem: A college club buys a fund that copies a big market list (an index). What decides what it holds?

options.text: The index list and how much of each.
options.feedback: The fund tries to mirror the named basket, so its mix follows that rule.

options.text: A manager picking likely winners.
options.feedback: A fund manager may pick stocks in other funds. This fund tracks a set list instead.

options.text: Whatever stocks trend online.
options.feedback: Online buzz does not set this fund's holdings. It follows the index list and its weights.

items.stem: At the family shop, Tara compares one company's share with an index fund of many firms. Which spreads risk more?

options.text: The fund of many companies.
options.feedback: One firm can stumble alone; a broad basket spreads that specific event.

options.text: The single share.
options.feedback: A single winner can look strong. One firm's trouble also reaches the whole holding.

options.text: Both equally.
options.feedback: One share rests on one firm. A fund holding many firms spreads that company risk much more widely.

items.stem: Managers pick stocks to beat an index. In one Indian year, about what percent of large-company funds did worse?

options.text: About 75 percent.
options.feedback: The scorecard reports 75% for this group and year. Active selection can trail an index; this figure is not a forecast.

options.text: About 25 percent.
options.feedback: That is the share left after 75% trailed. The cited result challenges the idea that stock picking usually won in this group.

options.text: About 50 percent.
options.feedback: Half is a natural guess, but the cited scorecard reports about 75% trailing for this group and year.

items.stem: What is an index fund trying to do?

options.text: Follow a named list of companies.
options.feedback: Its stated job is to follow an index, allowing for fees and tracking gaps.

options.text: Pick winners before the index changes.
options.feedback: That sounds like an active strategy, but an index fund aims to track its index rather than forecast winners.

options.text: Promise a fixed yearly return.
options.feedback: No index fund promises a set return. It tracks its index, so it shares the index's falls too.

items.stem: Arjun points to one winning share and says picking stocks always beats an index. Why is that weak?

options.text: One winner is not the typical result.
options.feedback: The selected success leaves out other picks and the cost of choosing them.

options.text: One winning share shows pickers usually win.
options.feedback: A winner is vivid. One case tells us little about the full set of picks.

options.text: One example settles all future markets.
options.feedback: One winner is easy to recall. It cannot tell how all picks fared over time.

items.stem: An index fund's expense ratio is a ___ taken out of the fund's money.

options.text: Cost.
options.feedback: The fund’s return to holders is affected by fees even when it tracks well.

options.text: One-time charge paid only on gains.
options.feedback: A fee may look tied to successful returns, but the expense ratio is charged from fund assets regardless of a gain.

options.text: Bonus.
options.feedback: A bonus is extra money paid out. The expense ratio is a cost taken from the fund's assets.

items.stem: Asha says past data prove no manager can beat an index. What goes too far?

options.text: Some managers did beat their index.
options.feedback: The data show a group trend. Some funds still beat their index.

options.text: Past group results set every future year.
options.feedback: A large study can feel final. Its past results do not set each new year's outcome.

options.text: Some beat it, so the group result means nothing.
options.feedback: A few winners do not erase the group result. The study still found many funds below their benchmark.

items.stem: Which line compares an index fund with one picked stock?

options.text: Following a whole list vs betting on one firm.
options.feedback: The first follows an index after costs; the second rests on one company’s result.

options.text: Both spread risk across many firms.
options.feedback: A broad fund can spread company risk, but one picked share still depends on that one company.

options.text: The index fund rests on one company's result.
options.feedback: That is backwards. The single stock rests on one company, while the fund follows a whole index.

misconceptions.name: Index means guaranteed growth
misconceptions.correction: Tracking a market index also means sharing its falls.

misconceptions.name: One winner proves a method
misconceptions.correction: One strong stock says little about the average result of many picks.

quest.title: Compare baskets
quest.detail: Compare the holdings and fees in two made-up fund fact sheets.

concepts.title: UPI scams and social engineering
concepts.hook: A fake prize message may ask for a UPI PIN to make a payment look like a receipt.
concepts.rule: A scam story can steer a person to approve a payment. A UPI PIN lets money leave an account.

claims.text: NPCI warns that a QR scan and UPI PIN can be used to make a payment, not collect a prize.
A collect request asks the payer to approve money leaving an account.

items.stem: A caller tells a hostel student to scan a QR code and enter her UPI PIN for a refund. What does this do?

options.text: It approves money going out.
options.feedback: NPCI says a QR scan with a PIN is for paying, not receiving a refund.

options.text: It checks the sender has enough money.
options.feedback: The PIN step can sound like a safety check. It can approve money leaving instead.

options.text: It lets the bank send her the refund.
options.feedback: A refund sounds like cash coming in. A PIN can send cash out instead.

items.stem: At a college fest, a caller asks Priya to approve a collect request for a prize. What is he asking for?

options.text: Permission for a payment.
options.feedback: The word collect can hide that the person approving it is the payer.

options.text: Proof the prize will reach her account.
options.feedback: A prize message makes approval sound like a receipt step, but a collect request asks the payer to authorise money leaving.

options.text: A survey about the fest.
options.feedback: A collect request is not a survey. Approving it with a PIN lets money leave the payer's account.

items.stem: A fake message promises ₹200 cashback but sends a ₹2,000 UPI collect request. If you enter your PIN, about what do you pay?

options.text: About ₹2,000.
options.feedback: The collect request asks the student to pay ₹2,000. The ₹200 promise does not change that amount.

options.text: About ₹200 comes in.
options.feedback: The cashback promise describes a receipt, but the ₹2,000 collect request asks you to pay.

options.text: About ₹1,800 leaves.
options.feedback: Subtracting the promised cashback assumes it arrives. The approved collect request is for the full ₹2,000.

items.stem: What does a UPI PIN mainly do?

options.text: Approves a payment from your account.
options.feedback: The PIN is entered when the payer approves a bank transaction.

options.text: Checks that a payment is about to arrive.
options.feedback: The caller calls it a check to get cash. A PIN can send cash out.

options.text: Unlocking the payment app.
options.feedback: App unlock codes are separate. The UPI PIN is what approves money leaving a bank account.

items.stem: A neat message seems to come from a bank worker. Why can it still fool someone?

options.text: Its story can push you into a real payment.
options.feedback: The app can work well while a false story sways the person.

options.text: A bank-like tone proves the caller is safe.
options.feedback: A neat message can seem safe. The PIN still lets a payer send money out.

options.text: The logo proves the PIN only receives money.
options.feedback: A bank mark can feel safe. The PIN can still approve money going out.

items.stem: A stranger sends you a collect request. If you enter your PIN to approve it, whose account pays?

options.text: Yours, the one that approves.
options.feedback: Entering your PIN on a collect request approves money leaving your own linked account.

options.text: The stranger's, who asked to collect.
options.feedback: The requester is asking to receive money. The person who approves with a PIN pays.

options.text: No one's; it is only a request.
options.feedback: A request turns into a payment once the PIN is entered. The money then leaves the account of whoever approves.

items.stem: Jay says every UPI scam needs a hacked app. What is he missing?

options.text: People can be tricked into real payments.
options.feedback: The bank may send the money as asked. The story can still be false.

options.text: An official-looking request cannot be a scam.
options.feedback: The bank style can win trust. A false story can still lead to a real payment.

options.text: An app must be hacked before money leaves.
options.feedback: An app hack may sound like the only risk. A scammer can also trick you into paying.

items.stem: Which line best sums up a UPI payment trick?

options.text: A false story gets a real payment approved.
options.feedback: The attacker targets a choice on the screen rather than changing the PIN’s job.

options.text: The PIN turns into a receipt code.
options.feedback: The scam calls the PIN a receipt code. The code still approves money going out.

options.text: The scammer changes the bank's PIN rules.
options.feedback: The PIN rules stay the same. The trick works by steering a person to approve a real payment.

misconceptions.name: PIN to receive
misconceptions.correction: To get money, a person need not key in a UPI PIN.

misconceptions.name: Official tone proves safety
misconceptions.correction: A neat bank-like note can still tell a false story.

quest.detail: In a made-up payment screen, identify the payer and the direction of money.
